A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, renamed from MoCo to MoSA, with shared authors, framework and MoVid dataset. Their text, figures, tables, equations and appendices support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original generation experiments, component and dataset ablations, dataset analyses and user studies, including Tables 1–5 and G–L.

after.justification: v2 reports original quantitative comparisons and user studies, alongside contact-constraint, backbone-transfer, camera-view and HumanVid animation experiments.

M1.justification: v2 adds a 3D contact loss to the training objective and introduces image-to-video and pose-driven variants, with the latter omitting the 3D generator. The motion-generator specification also changes from MARDM's CLIP-conditioned diffusion-MLP pipeline in v1 Appendix D to text-tokenized autoregressive motion generation in v2 Appendix A. These extend the procedure beyond renaming.

E1.justification: v2 adds pose-driven animation training and evaluation on HumanVid, beyond its retained role as alternative training data in v1's dataset ablation. Appendices F–H additionally demonstrate changing camera trajectories, half-body and multi-person generation, and image-conditioned generation. These broaden task and input-condition coverage; MoVid remains a 30K-video dataset.

E2.justification: v2 adds qualitative comparisons with Kling and Seedance, evaluates Champ in the new HumanVid animation comparison, and adds HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1 to the general-model user study. HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1 were already quantitatively evaluated in v1 Table L; their consolidation into v2 Table 1 is not a new comparator addition.

E3.justification: The new HumanVid experiment specifies shared training/test sets, prompts and pose conditions, adding SSIM, PSNR, LPIPS and FID metrics. The image-to-video variant introduces random-frame image conditioning and skeleton translation/scaling augmentation. Camera testing adds two fixed views and two changing trajectories. The existing 720×480 resolution, 20,000 iterations and batch size of 16 are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds backbone-transfer testing on Wan2.1, contact-constraint ablation with a penetration example, and camera-view robustness analysis (Tables 2, 3 and 13; Figures 4, 13 and 15). Existing structure, HADC, tracking and dataset ablations remain, although discussions move. Conversely, v1 Table H's comparison of MLD, T2M-GPT and MARDM as alternative structure generators is removed.

E5.justification: v1 checklist item 7 explicitly discloses fixed random variables such as seeds and avoidance of multiple seeds because of computational cost. v2 removes this disclosure. Neither version reports error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests; the deletion does not establish that the underlying run or seed policy changed.

E6.justification: Table 1's proposed-method FVD/CLIPSIM change from 1108/0.3021 to 1093/0.3035, while subject consistency changes from 97.74% to 96.83%, under the revised method. Ablation values also change, and new backbone, contact, HumanVid animation and camera results appear. General-model preference percentages are replaced after expanding the choice set, preventing direct percentage comparisons. Alternative-generator results and whole-body video counts are removed.

T1.justification: v2 Appendix B adds mathematical definitions for human/scene point sets, penetrating points and a piecewise signed-distance contact penalty in Equation 10; Equation 9 incorporates this additional loss. This is a localized extension of the mathematical formulation. The existing diffusion, HADC and tracking objectives remain substantially unchanged, and no theorems or proofs are added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion elevate human–environment interaction handling through the contact constraint into a central contribution. The introduction also broadens the framing from text-driven generation to text or image prompts. Structure–appearance decoupling, HADC, dense tracking and MoVid remain core contributions, but the claimed capability scope expands substantially.

C2.justification: v1 Section 7 identifies complex human–scene interactions as a limitation deferred to future work. v2 removes that discussion and interprets its contact ablation as evidence of reduced penetration. It adds interpretations concerning backbone transferability, camera-view robustness and broader generation capabilities, plus a specific qualification about limited commercial-model evaluation. The earlier interpretation of robustness across alternative motion generators disappears.

D1.justification: Most training details remain unchanged. v2 adds contact implementation specifics, including VGGT, a zero penetration threshold and loss weight 10.0, plus image-conditioning and augmentation instructions. It omits v1's eight-structure-block setting and approximately 10-second structure-generation estimate. Both versions describe supplementary code and samples; v2 additionally states planned research-use restrictions for the dataset.

R1.justification: The related-work scope remains broadly similar, with selective citation and attribution changes. v2 adds works including Go to Zero, MoMask, RealisMotion, VGGT and MagCache, while removing conditional-control references such as ControlNet and ControlNeXt that motivated v1's copied transformer blocks. Most human-video and motion-generation positioning is retained.

P1.justification: Beyond renaming MoCo to MoSA, v2 substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction and contribution statement and reorganizes the document. Implementation details and several ablation discussions move into an expanded appendix, references move before the appendix, and the NeurIPS checklist is replaced by separate ethics, reproducibility and LLM-use statements.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is substantially redrawn with attention-block and text-flow details. v1 Tables 1/L are consolidated into v2 Table 1, while dataset Tables F/G become Table 8 with a revised column structure. v2 adds a motion-transformer diagram, dataset examples and numerous comparison, contact, camera and generation-variant figures, while relocating existing ablation visuals.

improvement.justification: The contact ablation addresses the interaction weakness acknowledged in v1, while the Wan2.1 transfer test and matched HumanVid evaluation strengthen evidence for applicability (v2 Tables 2, 3 and 12; Figure 13). These benefits support a limited net improvement. Reporting losses temper the gain: fixed-seed and eight-block disclosures disappear, and Table 11 retains v1's 1108/0.3021 result without explaining its relationship to Table 1's revised 1093/0.3035 result.
